The first volume of the Canon of Medicine,
composed by the Chief Master Abu Ali al-Husayn ibn Sina al-Bukhari.
It contains:
The First Book,
which concerns the Universals (general principles of medicine),
and the Second Book,
on simple (compound) drugs.

Right page:

In the name of God, the Merciful, the Compassionate, and may God's blessings be upon our master Muhammad the Noble.
Praise be to God with praise befitting His abundant grace, and blessings upon Muhammad and his family and servants. I have sought to extract for myself, and for one who has not found a name for himself in medicine, a way to seek healing through reference to universal principles and particular things, so as not to need to gather rare ingredients or go without fulfilling most needs.
To make this accessible, I resolved not to speak of matters in their totality in general terms. First I will describe the natural methods of medicine, then after that the universal principles and properties of simple drugs, then their combinations, then after that the diseases occurring in each organ, beginning first with a description of that organ and its function. The primary organs and their simple drugs first, then the description thereof, which is in the first book — the kidneys and likewise the description of their functions — then when I have finished describing that organ...

Left page:

I begin the most important sections by mentioning how to preserve health, then follow that with a universal statement of its requirements, causes, methods of reasoning about them, and ways to address them. Having dealt with these universal matters, I move to particular diseases, mentioning them also under the universal headings, and then — God willing — detailing them. Then come the universal laws, then the treatments, then I descend to particular matters of simple and compound remedies, those whose composition comes from simple drugs, and the matters of simple drugs. Then when dealing with small quantities and the uses of pigments in their application, when I reach that point, even if the universal details are few, and what are compound medicines — the other kind — when tested, I believe that the learned will understand their composition and how to mix them. I resolved that when I finish this, the book will be a complete work. Also, particular matters not specifically concerned with diseases will be mentioned there as well, along with discussion of related topics also in this book, following the method of the abridged book. When this book is finished, and if God grants me the ability to complete it, I regard it as a book unmatched by any other, and this book is not for those who are weak in the art. THE FIRST CHAPTER OF THE BOOK OF UNIVERSALS IN MEDICINE

The first thing we ought to know at the outset concerns the states of the human being, in terms of health and its departure, and the descent into illness. One might say that medicine is divided into theory and practice, so that every theoretical element could be called a science. We must say that it is said that among the arts there are those that are theoretical and those that are practical, just as this is said of philosophy — that medicine has a theoretical part and a practical part. The meaning in each division of the terms "theoretical" and "practical" is something other than the general philosophical usage; this applies specifically to medicine. It must be made clear that part of medicine is theoretical in nature, dealing with knowledge and instruction, while another part is practical. This is clarified by those who have examined this subject. We should know that this means something further: no one of the premises of medicine can stand alone as pure knowledge — rather, it functions as a report about how one approaches the first principles, what is called "knowledge" or "theory," while the second is called "practice" in terms of what actually brings the theoretical conviction into reality. Among the matters of conviction it is said that medicine, when its methods are compared, has instruction as its second component, while practical action leads toward causes and measures that are limitless. All of this is organized under the division of medical knowledge, since instruction in medicine begins when it is connected to the manner of application.

Left page:

As is said in medicine, the matters that must be examined concern the conditions that are necessary for the human being to maintain health and prevent its loss, and how this is to be achieved. Certain ideas emerge from this, supported by established principles, having to do with the analysis of compounds and medications, and with the composition from materials that pertain to the natural organs — all of which is encompassed in this knowledge. One must explain in what manner the knowledge of these things is attained. It must also be stated that we are speaking about a single aspect of the states of the human body. In what follows we shall mention that disease and its variations are classified according to the active principle involved. Between these two positions there is no room for an intermediate path, nor for incidental occurrences. We further state that in discussing deficiency one must account for disease in relation to the three states we have established: direct contact, illness itself — which encompasses the functions that have deviated from their proper origins — and the normal balanced state, as well as its opposite. Regarding these realities, one must verify deficiency and the conditions stipulated, without involving ourselves in a dispute among physicians on this point, for this is not something they contest in the same way, nor does it lead anywhere. Its benefit in medicine is to verify these matters for those who adhere to the principles of the art.

THE SECOND CHAPTER ON THE SUBJECT OF MEDICINE

Since medicine examines the states of health and illness from the standpoint of both knowledge and practice in a comprehensive manner, it achieves its full value only when the underlying causes are known — for one cannot truly learn medicine without knowing its causes.

Right page:

Health and disease, since health and disease may be manifest or hidden, and we do not reach them except by inference from their symptoms, it is necessary for the physician first to know how to identify health and disease. We have previously established that true knowledge is that which is acquired concerning causes, and that if things have essential concomitants, things fall into four categories: material, efficient, formal, and receptive. The material causes in things that relate to health and disease are the proximate subject matter. As for the subject of the humors, these are the efficient causes. As for the elements, they serve as the substrate in two respects according to composition. Even if the qualities are of all kinds, they come together in their composition. The discussion of this subject involves three things: the temperament, the constitution as it pertains to the body's condition, and the structure as it pertains to composition. As for the efficient causes, they operate in two senses: first, the preservation of the human body from harm and what is connected to it, such as food, water, and beverages, and what is related to them — evacuation, retention, regions, and dwellings, and what is connected to them — bodily and psychic motions and rest, among them sleep, wakefulness, and retention.

Left page:

In the human being and the differences therein, and in the species, arts, habits, and things that act upon the body — whether by opposing nature or by following nature — as for the formal causes, they are the temperaments, the faculties that arise from them, the composite structure, and the receptive causes which are the actions. In knowing the actions, one knows the faculties in their states, and knowledge of the spirits that carry the faculties is among the foundations. These are the subjects of the art of medicine: what the physician aims at with respect to the human body is to preserve it and to remove disease. It is therefore necessary that the causes be divided into those that precede and those that follow, and the causes are of three kinds. The removal of disease is first by choosing favorable air, then by regulating motion and rest, by treating the disease, and the physicians according to their three categories: those concerned with treatment and disease, and those in between, who are mentioned as intermediaries between two classes, with no true middle ground between them. If we were to enumerate all of this in detail, we would have shown it completely. In sum, medicine examines the elements, temperaments, humors, simple and compound organs, the spirits and their natural, psychic, and vital faculties and actions, states of health and disease, and what causes and maintains them — including foods, beverages, waters, regions, dwellings, evacuations, retentions, putrefactions, crafts, and activities.

Right page:

Concerning bodily and psychological movements, constitutions, and what is required of the body in terms of external matters, management of food and drink, preservation of air, care of movement and constitution, medicines, and the general conditions for preserving health and treating disease. Some of these matters require the physician to conceptualize and know them truly and with active conviction, based on what is accepted from the sound principles of natural science. Some require him to practice them in his craft. If they are among the foundational principles, he must follow them, for the principles of particular sciences are established and demonstrated in the general sciences, and from these all the principles of the sciences ascend to First Philosophy, which we encounter after natural science. When some practitioners rush and err in establishing these foundations, they go wrong in the subject of natural science, introducing into medical practice what does not belong to it, making errors in explanation. The physician must therefore form a conceptual understanding of the essence of things, and from this will derive the elements, temperaments, their qualities, and every condition, causes, organs and their benefits.

Left page:

As for treatment by sense and experience: those who respond to these describe and demonstrate diseases, their causes and symptoms, how illness progresses, and how health is preserved. All that is demonstrated through this method is worked out in detail, sequentially, and with proper timing. But if one attempts to establish proofs for everything, he does so as a philosopher rather than a physician, and his discourse comes from natural philosophy rather than from medicine. If he attempts to demonstrate the validity of inference through method, he does so from a methodological standpoint, which belongs to the physician as physician.

The Second Lesson: The Elements
The subject of this science is one of the elements found in simple, primary bodies of the human body and others, which cannot be divided into bodies of different forms and cannot be mixed. The different types among natural bodies are of four kinds: two light and two heavy. The two light ones are fire and air; the two heavy ones are earth and water. The earth is a simple body whose natural place is the center of all existing things. Nature moves toward it when separated from it by its own absolute action. It is cold and moist by nature when what requires this emerges, even without an external cause outside its nature.

[Right page:]
It is perceptible, and its existence in created things is as a substrate for forms and stable qualities, and for the preservation of shapes and configurations. As for Water, it is a simple body whose natural place is a sphere encompassing the earth, itself encompassed by air, when it is in its natural position. It receives and is cold and moist in its nature; when mixed, it accepts form. Whatever opposes it causes, by external means, a perceptible coldness to appear from it, and it flows with moisture, and forms in its totality where required. It serves as the first recipient and accepts form, but does not preserve it. Its existence in created things enables the continuation of configurations, for the material parts of forms, through shaping, preservation, and modification. If something is easily disposed to receive forms, it is apt to receive the dry; and if it is difficult for forms to be received, it is reluctant to release them — this is what draws the dry-moist together. The dry lends itself to shaping; medicine attests to this. The dry preserves what has been formed and is close to the modification of moisture. As for Air, it is a simple body whose natural place is above water and below the concavity of the fiery sphere; its nature is warm and moist. Its existence in created things causes dissolution, refinement, lightness, and movement. As for Fire, it is a simple body whose natural place is above all other elements.

[Left page:]
Its natural place is the concave surface of the innermost sphere, adjacent to the region of generation and corruption. This is established by its absolute quality and its hot temperament. Its existence in created things brings about ripening and maturation. Through it, the souls of living things are sustained, and through it, the active faculty is enabled to work upon matter. From this arise the temperamental and natural faculties of created beings, their stability, and their activation. Through it, the limbs are moved and their functions sustained. The first section concerns the elements.

The First Section: The Method — How the interaction of mutually opposing parts occurs. These opposing parts exist within a unified body, concentrated and acting upon one another. They spread through the whole of the body so that it becomes uniform in all its parts, with neither a distinct temperament nor a primary quality prevailing. The four primary qualities present in the four aforementioned elements — heat, cold, moisture, and dryness — interact in bodies and created things when they come into contact with one another. The practical consideration, taken absolutely without qualification and in its proper sense, is that the temperament becomes a universal measure for all the opposing qualities, so that the opposing qualities in the compound become equal and balanced, and the temperament stands as a mean between them. The second type of temperament exists between mutually opposing qualities in an absolute and intermediate sense, yet inclines toward one of the two extremes.

Right page:

As for one of the two opposites, they are coldness and heat, and moisture and dryness, and as for their lesser forms — but what is truly considered in the art of medicine is the state of equilibrium and deviation from equilibrium. Neither this nor that is the way to proceed. Rather, the physician must know what constitutes the natural temperament and equilibrium, and understand that it is possible to find instead of it the temperament of a human being or the temperament of an organ, even if it is far from the balanced and equalized state. The equilibrium is derived from those who speak of balance, meaning proportionality and equalization. Rather, from the indicated divisions, it means that the temperament has been fully realized with the proper amounts and qualities of the elements in their quantities and qualities, as is required for the precise temperament of the human being. In terms of proportion and degree, it may happen that from a given portion, the two are very close to the true equilibrium — the primary one. This approximate equilibrium, which is necessary, is what people also call the relative standard of measurement, which is different from that absolute equilibrium. For this reason, it is not possible for a person to attain the equilibrium mentioned in the first aspect, so there are eight aspects of consideration for it: First, it may be measured for the species as measured against what is external to it; or it may be measured for the species as measured against what differs within it; or it may be measured from one type as measured against what is external to it that differs.

Left page:

And within its species. Or it may be measured according to its type within the species as compared to what differs within it. Or it may be measured according to the particular member of the type as compared to what differs and is external to it and its type and species. Or it may be measured according to the particular member as compared to what differs from its own states. Or it may be measured according to what is compounded with it as compared to what differs from what is external to it and is derived from it. Or it may be measured according to what is compounded as compared to its own states within it. The first division is the absolute true equilibrium, which is the standard of measurement in general — since it pertains to all — and one should not be too lenient about it, and one should also follow the standard without excess. Closest to it are those two: a human being whose temperament is modeled on the temperament of a human, and the third is the mean between temperaments. Through this, the particular characteristic of the utmost equilibrium is distinguished, which is the perfection of balance — the age at which one reaches the fullness of strength. This too is close to, but not exactly, the true equilibrium, and this likewise does not truly exist. However, it is established in one in whom the hot organs such as the heart, and the cold ones such as the brain, and the natural ones such as the liver, and the structural ones such as the bones are all in balance and proportion. When they are balanced and equalized, one is close to the true equilibrium, since the equilibrium of each organ is like that of every other organ. This is the perfection, subject to the condition that there must also be a relation to the vital spirits and to the other relationships of rank. After that, it would be approximating the true equilibrium, though still outside it.

Marginal note:
This also applies because the true equilibrium constituted by the full actualization of its proper functions in succession is possible in its existence.

Right page:

Concerning heat and moisture: the source of life is the heart and the vital spirit, and when these incline toward excess, the body cannot sustain life through heat and moisture alone, for it is heat that maintains the spirit and nourishes it. The principal organs are three, as previously mentioned, and the coldest among them is the brain; and it does not suit the heart if the heat of the heart is not tempered, for the heart tends toward dryness; and the heart's dryness cannot be compensated by the moisture of the brain and liver, nor can the brain compensate the liver in this way either, nor does the heart's temperament suit one that is dry. The brain is the fourth among them. As for the Third Section:

This is a temperament derived from the first, which is the ideal, but it possesses a relative equilibrium suited to a particular people according to their climate and region. These are the people whose temperament inclines toward deviation from the ideal, each measured by reference to their own nature. As for comparison by country: if one considers the temperament of a Macedonian measured against India, and likewise the condition of an independent country against the temperament of an Indian, then each one is well-suited and adequate — each having a temperament fitting and appropriate to its own climate, though it has extremes of excess and deficiency.
